text.p: Germany's Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG, which last week reported a 90 percent slump in 1996 net profit due to a steep rise in loan provisions, on Monday forecast earnings would recover this year.

Germany's sixth-largest listed bank, which is considering a merger with Norddeutsche Landesbank, said operating profit after provisions would rise back towards one billion marks ($580.9 million) after sliding 63 percent to 355 million marks in 1996.
It also intends to keep its dividend unchanged for 1997 at 1.10 marks, the same level as 1996 and 1995.

The state-owed bank reported on Friday that net profit slumped to 47 million marks, a tenth of the previous year's level, as the bank more than doubled its risk provisions to 2.5 billion marks to cover problem corporate loans, primarily at its subsidiary Berliner Bank.

The bank is in the middle of an overhaul which will include shedding 10 percent of its 17,000 staff in 1997 and 1998 and closing branches, Wolfgang Rupf, who took over as chief executive at the start of 1997, told a news conference.
"It was a shock for me how high the need for risk provisioning really was," said Rupf, who joined Bankgesellschaft's management board last November.
Berliner Bank would in future avoid taking on large individual loan risks. It had suffered some large corporate loan losses, including severeal which resulted from "criminal intent," Rupf said.
A reorganisation designed to improve risk management and make the decentralised group easier to steer should be completed by mid-1997.
The group has been hit by an economic downturn in its home region of Berlin and east Germany and Rupf said there were no signs of any big improvement soon.
He predicted business would be satisfactory in 1997 after operating profit before provisions rose at a double-digit percentage rate in the first quarter.
"If we were a ship I'd say that we have managed to pull ourselves off the reef," Rupf said.
Net interest and net commission income in the first quarter of 1997 matched the year-earlier levels, while own-account trading profit was well up.

The bank's upbeat outlook had little impact on its share price which closed down five pfennigs at 32.75 marks. It outperformed most other major banks which showed heavier losses in line with the market as a whole.
Rupf said Bankgesellschaft was only able to post a net profit for 1996 because it took 240 million marks from reserves to pay for the dividend and sold real estate worth 174 million marks.
He said Bankgesellschaft was in favour in principle of a link-up with state-owned regional bank Norddeutsche Landesbank and that a decision on whether to proceed was likely this year.

In a move which fuelled speculation about mergers in Germany's overcrowded banking sector, Bankgesellschaft and Norddeutsche Landesbank last year got the go-ahead from their state owners to intensify talks about increasing cooperation.

Rupf said competition in the German banking sector would grow ahead of European monetary union in 1999, especially as non-banks like industrial companies or credit card firms pushed into traditional banking markets.
"The wave of mergers of big banks that long ago started in other countries will also reach Germany, Rupf said.
